transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (Lighthouse VP Eng), Claire Morgan (Cloud Architect), Elliot Reed (Security), Ava Kim (PM)

Summary (auto-gen): Initial discovery for Private/VPC deployment; main concerns are network connectivity (peering vs private endpoints), allowed regions, key management, and audit logging. Next steps captured at end.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for making time. i'm maya from redwood, i'm the account exec for lighthouse. quick intros - i'll hand off to diego for the technical bits.
[00:12] Sanjay: hey maya, sanjay here. thanks. happy to go over what we're looking for.
[00:18] Claire: claire - cloud architect. primarily interested in the network and dns pieces.
[00:22] Elliot: elliot, security. i'll be focused on keys, logs, and egress controls.
[00:27] Diego: great thanks. uh quick agenda: we'll do a short discovery on current infra, then dig into the private deployment options - vpc peering, private endpoints (privatelink), transit gateway - and cover region constraints and key mgmt.

[00:45] Maya: one note - i'll drop links after the call: private-vpc-arch (https://redwood.ai/docs/private-vpc-arch) and our security packet.

[01:05] Sanjay: for context: we run a multi-account aws setup in us-east-1 and us-west-2, dev in us-west-2, prod in us-east-1. we're evaluating redwood because we want consistent latency for inference but with data never leaving our VPCs. also looking at some dedicated vendors and a possible in-house option.
[01:22] Diego: okay, that helps. do you plan to expose a private endpoint per region or peer to a central redwood account?
[01:31] Claire: ideally per region. we want traffic to stay local - so us-east-1 connections should not route to west. also something about cross-account peering limits we hit before.
[01:45] Maya: yep, per-region private endpoints is a common ask. we support both models: 1) per-region private endpoint (aws privatelink / endpoint service), 2) peering to a redwood tenant vpc, 3) transit gateway for large scale - each has tradeoffs.

[02:05] Diego: the rough networking tradeoffs: privatelink gives you an ENI in your account and strong isolation, but each endpoint is per-region and per-service - more setup. vpc peering is simpler but you can't do transitive routing and there are cidr overlap concerns. transit gateway scales better for many accounts but you need to manage route tables.
[02:28] Claire: what about egress and internet access - we need to ensure inference traffic never traverses public internet and egress is controlled.
[02:35] Diego: absolutely. with privatelink, traffic stays on aws backbone; with peering also stays internal. we can optionally terminate TLS at the customer side or inside the redwood runtime depending on the keying.

[02:50] Elliot: on keys - we need kms or hsm integration. can redwood use our customer-managed keys? we can't have plaintext keys stored by third parties.
[02:58] Maya: yes, we support BYOK via aws kms with cross-account grants; for on-prem / air-gapped we have hsm integration options. diego can outline the exact flow.
[03:12] Diego: technically, we request a grant on the CMK to allow the redwood service principal to decrypt. the keys remain in your account; we never export key material. note: permissions are required for encrypt/decrypt on the specific CMK alias used for model payloads. sometimes the document shows this as 'service principal grant', and we can provide the policy snippet.

[03:38] Claire: does that work with internal proxy / egress proxies? we route all outbound through an egress proxy for inspection.
[03:46] Diego: yes - we can route out through your existing proxy; the private endpoint/peering will appear as internal traffic and you can apply the same inspection policies. one caveat: for privatelink the aws endpoint uses an ENI and the source ip will be from your VPC - so the proxy setup should accept that.

[04:05] Sanjay: region constraints - we run in gov-cloud like pockets? not govcloud, but we have a dedicated eu-west-1 tenant and some regulatory data that can't leave eu-west-1. can redwood host private endpoints in eu-west-1?
[04:18] Maya: yes, we have private deployment options in several public regions including eu-west-1. for restricted data we recommend deploying a regional private control plane or dedicated capacity pinned to the region.

[04:30] Claire: is there multi-region replication for model state or cache? if we pin to a region will we need multiple deployments for cross-region users?
[04:39] Diego: currently our KV cache and runtime state are region-local. if you need sub-100ms latencies globally, you'd run instances in each region. we support automated routing rules so requests hit the nearest regional endpoint. there is a replication story for metadata but model KV cache is per-region to avoid cross-region latency.

[05:05] Elliot: audit logs - we need immutable logs forwarded to our splunk/s3 bucket, and retention of 7 years for certain events. can redwood stream logs to our central account?
[05:17] Maya: yes, we can forward audit logs (request/response metadata, not user payloads by default) to a customer s3 bucket or splunk via Kinesis/Firehose. payload-level logs need explicit customer permission and are usually restricted. we'll share the log schema.

[05:35] Sanjay: any network port requirements or security groups we should prepare?
[05:39] Diego: standard privatelink ports - HTTPS (443) is used for the control plane + data plane. for peering, it's also 443. we may ask you to allow certain IP ranges if using peering with NAT egress. we'll provide a one-page network checklist.

[05:58] Ava: question - what's the onboarding timeline for a pilot? we are hoping to have a POC within two weeks.
[06:05] Maya: typical is 1-2 weeks for a minimal pilot once networking is in place. the blocker is usually getting VPC CIDRs and IAM roles configured. if we can get the CIDR ranges and a service account we can target kickoff next week.

[06:20] Claire: cross-account IAM patterns - do you require an IAM role in our account or do you assume a role?
[06:26] Diego: we generally prefer a cross-account IAM role with a restricted policy for the things we need (kms:Decrypt grant via key policy + s3:PutObject for logs if streaming). alternatively, for privatelink we can minimize IAM interactions; it's mainly networking and the key grant.

[06:44] Sanjay: any gotchas with overlapping CIDRs? we've historically had overlap across some partner accounts.
[06:50] Diego: that will block peering. privatelink is more tolerant (since it uses ENIs and doesn't require unique CIDR), so if you have overlap privatelink may be preferred. we'll ask for your CIDR list to recommend the best approach.

[07:05] Elliot: compliance - we need SOC2 and ISO docs and an incident response runbook.
[07:10] Maya: we'll share our compliance package and SOC2 report redacted. we also have an incident playbook we can discuss with security.

[07:20] Diego: one technical detail: our runtime supports TLS mutual auth for the data plane if you prefer mTLS; some customers use client certs in addition to the privatelink. this gives an extra layer in case of misconfig.

[07:36] Claire: about dns - will the privatelink set up private dns entries in our route53?
[07:41] Diego: yes we can optionally configure private hosted zone entries that resolve the redwood endpoint to the ENI IPs. customers often prefer that to avoid having to change callers.

[07:55] Sanjay: ok can you give a quick mapping of recommended approach for our setup: multi-account, us-east-1 and us-west-2, some eu-west assets, internal proxy - what's your recommendation?
[08:05] Diego: recommendation: start with privatelink per region for prod-critical workloads (eu-west-1 and us-east-1) to avoid CIDR overlap and get strong isolation. use peering or transit gateway for internal dev/test where scale is higher and you control CIDRs. pin dedicated capacity in eu-west-1 for regulatory data.

[08:28] Maya: and pricing note - privatelink setup has a small infra cost per endpoint plus data processing; dedicated capacity pricing is heavier but gives guaranteed throughput; we'll send a rough comparison.

[08:40] Ava: about monitoring - can we get per-request latency metrics and token-level cost breakdown per model?
[08:46] Maya: yes, our console provides token-level cost/latency breakdown and per-route dashboards. we can also stream metrics to your prometheus/grafana via pushgateway or a metrics collector.

[09:00] Claire: any required ports for egress to your control plane or updates? we have tight egress controls and want to whitelist only required endpoints.
[09:07] Diego: we'll provide a minimal list: control-plane endpoints (region-specific) on 443, and optionally S3/KMS endpoints if you allow log uploads. all over TLS.

[09:20] Elliot: about data retention - we must ensure that no customer PII is stored longer than necessary. can redwood confirm default retention?
[09:28] Maya: default is ephemeral - we don't store request payloads by default. audit logs are metadata and can be configured for retention. if you require zero retention we can work out a config where we never log payloads and rotate metadata frequently.

[09:45] Sanjay: ok final few items - for the POC what does success look like?
[09:50] Ava: we want baseline latency numbers in region (p50/p95), throughput for our expected qps (we're planning 150 qps bursty), and validation that keys & logs meet our security bar.
[10:02] Diego: noted. we'll run a benchmark with sample prompts; i'll produce a script that hits the endpoints and records p50/p95 and token costs.

[10:15] Maya: recap / next steps: i'll send the private deployment doc and compliance packet, diego will share the perf checklist and script, claire will share VPC details, elliot will confirm compliance items. schedule POC kickoff for week of 3/11 if networking is ready.

[10:35] Sanjay: sounds good. anything else?
[10:38] Claire: nope, thanks.

[10:40] Elliot: thanks everyone.

[10:43] Maya: thanks all - i'll email notes and links.
